newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: China warns Denmark on rights text amid EU discord.
newsitem.headline: China warns Denmark on rights text amid EU discord.

text.p: Denmark vowed on Monday to press ahead with a United Nations resolution criticising China's human rights record, defying Beijing's warning that the move would severely damage ties.

Assured of the backing of the United States and most European Union states, with the notable exceptions of France and Germany, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said his country would table the resolution, which is to be presented this week at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

Previous attempts to condemn China on human rights in a U.N. resolution following Beijing's bloody 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protesters have failed. China has rallied enough support each year to block the move.
Denmark's defiance drew immediate fire from Beijing, although officials also called for talks, not confrontation,

"If Denmark insists on doing this it will end up as the biggest loser," Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said. "I can say relations will be severely damaged in the political or economic and trade areas."

Liu Hainian, director of China's human rights centre and head of the Institute of Law at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told reporters: "China is a developing country and democracy has to be a gradual process."
Undeterred, Denmark's Petersen told the Danish Ritzaus news agency: "We have made our decision."
The Chinese bid to stop the Nordic nation from going ahead with the resolution came after EU discord thwarted attempts to agree a joint EU resolution.

EU heavyweight France declared last month it refused to back such a text, saying dialogue with Beijing was better than confrontation. Germany, Spain and Italy have since adopted a similar attitude, diplomats said.
"It is more important to achieve specific progress than to agree on resolutions which have no success," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told reporters.
The sensitive issue of human rights in China was debated by EU foreign ministers during a two-day meeting in the Dutch coastal town of Noordwijk.

The Dutch EU presidency had been expected to present the annual EU-sponsored resolution on behalf of all 15 members, but no consensus was found. However, Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said most EU countries supported the Danish-led resolution.
"We're grateful Denmark is willing to do this, and endorse the Danish resolution," he said, adding: "We are not targeting China in particular, but violations of human rights."
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in a statement on Saturday: "This decision by Denmark reflects its principled commitment to the universality of human rights."
The EU's failure to agree a joint resolution has sparked concerns about the EU's credibility on the world stage at a time when it seeks to strengthen its common foreign and security policy.
Van Mierlo has said failure to agree on the China motion was a serious setback for prospects of a common EU foreign policy.
"The EU needs to have a discussion about how it conducts itself in the United Nations on human rights issues," he said.
He also warned of applying double standards on human rights and taking a different approach towards large countries like China and smaller nations not as commercially important.
"This is not compatible with the universality of human rights," he said.
Van Mierlo said the EU would still press ahead with U.N. resolutions condemning the human rights records of countries such as Iraq, Iran and Burma.
"One mistake cannot be corrected by thousands of other mistakes," said Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama.
In Geneva on Sunday, diplomats said China had launched a rearguard action at the U.N. Human Rights Commission to head off the Danish resolution.
They said China was actively lobbying other countries to block the Danish resolution and that Beijing might succeed again.

The wording of the resolution had not yet been released but Petersen told Ritzau news agency that China should be criticised for its lack of respect for basic human rights such as freedom of assembly and speech.
